AI.method: MCMC parameter estimation using megamaser angular diameter distance and velocity measurements from the Megamaser Cosmology Project, applied to three f(R) models (HuSawicki, Starobinsky, ArcTanh) and ΛCDM, with model comparison via AIC and BIC.
AI.result: H₀ is constrained to ~73 km/s/Mpc across all models; b ≈ 0 for all f(R) models; Ωₘ is weakly constrained (~0.5); AIC/BIC show f(R) models are statistically indistinguishable from ΛCDM.
AI.conclusion: Megamaser data favors ΛCDM-like behavior in f(R) models, with no statistically significant deviation detected. The data cannot distinguish between these gravity models at current precision.

title: Hubble tension: the shape wall
comment: 24 pages, 18 sub-figures arranged into 4 figures, many references
summary: The standard "no-go theorem" against late-time solutions to the Hubble tension is essentially a normalization wall, since Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) measurements constrain the product $H_0r_d$, with $r_d$ the sound horizon at baryon drag. However, late-time solutions (which keep $r_d$ fixed) are tightly constrained not only by the BAO normalization $H_0r_d$, but also by the shape of the expansion history, i.e. the dimensionless expansion rate $E(z) \equiv H(z)/H_0$. We show that, if $r_d$ and the acoustic angular scale $θ_s$ are fixed, an increase in $H_0$ needs to be matched by an equal fractional increase in the dimensionless distance integral $I \equiv \int dz/E(z)$: $δH_0/H_0 \simeq δI/I$. We use this to quantify the "shape wall" set by relative distance constraints on $E(z)$, which we reconstruct nonparametrically, using Gaussian Processes and the latest unanchored Type Ia Supernovae (SNeIa) and BAO data. In our most conservative analysis using PantheonPlus SNeIa and DESI DR2 BAO data, we find a maximum fractional increase in $H_0$ of $\lesssim 2\%$, falling well short of the $\gtrsim 8\%$ required to solve the tension. This shape wall holds even in the presence of early-time new physics, and limits the maximum increase in $H_0$ which can be contributed by late-time modifications to $E(z)$ at fixed $θ_s$. Therefore, late-time modifications, whether invoked alone or alongside early-time new physics, face not only the well-known normalization wall, but also a stringent percent-level shape wall.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that late-time solutions to the Hubble tension face not only the previously known "normalization wall" from BAO calibration, but also a stringent "shape wall" from the dimensionless expansion rate E(z). Using Gaussian processes and unanchored SNeIa + BAO data (PantheonPlus + DESI DR2), they find that maximum H₀ increases from late-time modifications are ≤2%, far below the ~8% needed to resolve the tension. This constraint holds even with early-time new physics.
AI.motivation: To determine whether late-time (post-recombination) modifications to the expansion history can resolve the Hubble tension, given both the BAO normalization constraint (H₀r_d) and the shape constraint from the dimensionless expansion rate E(z).
AI.method: The authors derive an analytical relation linking fractional changes in H₀ to fractional changes in the dimensionless distance integral I ≡ ∫ dz/E(z) when r_d and θ_s are fixed. They then nonparametrically reconstruct E(z) using Gaussian Processes applied to unanchored Type Ia Supernovae (PantheonPlus) and BAO (DESI DR2) data, quantifying the allowed variation in H₀.
AI.result: The maximum fractional increase in H₀ from late-time modifications to E(z) is ≤2% in the most conservative analysis, far below the ≥8% needed to solve the Hubble tension. This "shape wall" persists even when early-time new physics is allowed.
AI.conclusion: Late-time modifications to the expansion history face a stringent percent-level "shape wall" from relative distance constraints, in addition to the known normalization wall. Even combined with early-time new physics, late-time modifications cannot sufficiently raise H₀ to resolve the tension.

title: Contribution to the 2026 Cosmology session of the 60th Rencontres de Moriond: Galactic moments: Understanding polarized foregrounds complexity in the quest for CMB primordial $B$ modes with LiteBIRD
summary: Accurate modeling of polarized Galactic emission has become a major challenge for current and next-generation cosmic microwave background (CMB) $B$-mode experiments. Ignoring the spectral complexity of thermal dust and Galactic synchrotron emission when integrating along the line of sight and over large sky fractions inevitably leads to biases in CMB polarization analyses. In this work, we review how the future LiteBIRD satellite, which will benefit from an increased number of bands and sensitivity with respect to past CMB experiments such as Planck, will exploit its broader frequency coverage to characterize the spectral properties of interstellar medium emission across the three-dimensional structure of the Milky Way. We show that the canonical description of foreground spectral behavior will reach its limits for LiteBIRD, and that this challenge can be addressed using the moment expansion formalism.

AI.tldr: LiteBIRD will use its broader frequency coverage to characterize polarized Galactic emission's spectral complexity via the moment expansion formalism, addressing biases in CMB B-mode analyses caused by oversimplified foreground models.
AI.motivation: Accurate modeling of polarized Galactic emission is a major challenge for CMB B-mode experiments; ignoring spectral complexity of dust and synchrotron emission leads to biases in CMB polarization analyses.
AI.method: Review of how LiteBIRD's increased number of bands and sensitivity compared to Planck will characterize spectral properties of interstellar medium emission across the Milky Way's 3D structure, using the moment expansion formalism.
AI.result: The canonical description of foreground spectral behavior will reach its limits for LiteBIRD; the moment expansion formalism can address this challenge.
AI.conclusion: LiteBIRD's broader frequency coverage enables improved foreground characterization, but new formalism (moment expansion) is needed to handle the spectral complexity beyond canonical models.

title: Web-Halo Model Peak-Background Split (WHM-PBS): halo bias as a distribution, not a number
summary: We present the Web--Halo Model Peak--Background Split (WHM-PBS), an analytic theory in which the large-scale bias of a dark-matter halo is inherited from its cosmic-web environment. Building on the Web--Halo Model, we use the Shen \textit{et al.} moving barriers for ellipsoidal collapse generating the web hierarchy in which every halo sits inside a host filament, itself inside a sheet. Combined with the peak--background split, this picture replaces the deterministic bias--mass relation $b(M_h)$ with the bias of the host environment, averaged over the conditional mass function. As a result, halo bias $b(M_h)$ is no longer a number but a strongly skewed \emph{distribution}. In this work we make use of this distribution in three different ways: as (i) a physically motivated prior on bias relations, (ii) a prediction on halo stochasticity, and (iii) a framework for assembly bias models. Regarding (i) we find that the density bias relations $b_2(b_1)$ and $b_3(b_1)$ stay tight, while the tidal bias $b_{s^2}(b_1)$ shows significant scatter, as found in $N$-body simulations. Regarding (ii), once including halo exclusion, our model reproduces the super- to sub-Poisson shot-noise trend of Baldauf \textit{et al.} which we convert into a prior band on the EFT stochasticity amplitude parameters. Finally, regarding (iii) in the density sector it explains the bias--concentration--correlation inversion of Paranjape \textit{et al.} at the characteristic mass ($M_\mathrm{h}\simeq1.7\times10^{13}\,h^{-1}\Msun$), with no parameter tuned to assembly bias.

AI.tldr: The WHM-PBS model explains halo bias as inherited from cosmic-web environments, producing a distribution of bias values rather than a single number. It reproduces key simulation results for bias relations, stochasticity, and assembly bias without parameter tuning.
AI.motivation: To develop an analytic theory that replaces the deterministic halo bias-mass relation with a distribution driven by cosmic-web environments, explaining observed scatter and assembly bias effects without ad-hoc tuning.
AI.method: Combines the Web-Halo Model (using Shen et al. moving barriers for ellipsoidal collapse) with the peak-background split, where each halo resides in a host filament inside a sheet. The bias of the host environment is averaged over the conditional mass function to produce a bias distribution.
AI.result: (i) Density bias relations b2(b1) and b3(b1) remain tight, while tidal bias b_{s^2}(b1) shows significant scatter (matching N-body). (ii) Reproduces super-to-sub-Poisson shot-noise trends (Baldauf et al.), yielding prior bands for EFT stochasticity parameters. (iii) Explains bias-concentration-correlation inversion (Paranjape et al.) at M_h~1.7e13 h-1 Msun with no tuned parameters.
AI.conclusion: The WHM-PBS provides a physically motivated framework connecting halo bias to cosmic-web environments, naturally producing stochasticity, non-linear bias relations, and assembly bias effects observed in simulations.

title: Hubble tension: a short review of theoretical explanations
comment: 49 pages, 13 figures, a short review prepared by invitation for RAA special topics
summary: The $Λ$ cold dark matter model successfully describes a wide range of cosmological observations. However, the persistent discrepancy between the value of the Hubble constant inferred from cosmic microwave background measurements within this model and that obtained from local distance-ladder determinations points to a significant inconsistency. This short review examines theoretical responses across the cosmological inference chain, from the gravitational field equations to the pre-recombination sound horizon and the late-time distance-redshift relation. We focus primarily on modified gravity, and briefly discuss early- and late-time mechanisms that can alter the acoustic ruler, distance measures, structure growth, or gravitational response. Current proposals can reduce the nominal tension, but often at the cost of correlated shifts in cosmic microwave background spectra, standard-ruler distances, lensing, structure growth, or calibrator information. Further progress requires unified likelihoods and multiprobe tests linking all key observables under the same model assumptions.

AI.tldr: This review examines theoretical responses to the Hubble constant tension, focusing on modified gravity and mechanisms altering the sound horizon, distance measures, structure growth, or gravitational response, concluding that progress requires unified multiprobe likelihoods under consistent model assumptions.
AI.motivation: The persistent discrepancy between the Hubble constant inferred from CMB measurements within ΛCDM and local distance-ladder determinations points to a significant inconsistency in the standard cosmological model.
AI.method: Short review examining theoretical responses across the cosmological inference chain, from gravitational field equations to pre-recombination sound horizon and late-time distance-redshift relation, focusing on modified gravity and early/late-time mechanisms.
AI.result: Current proposals can reduce nominal tension but often introduce correlated shifts in CMB spectra, standard-ruler distances, lensing, structure growth, or calibrator information.
AI.conclusion: Further progress requires unified likelihoods and multiprobe tests linking all key observables under the same model assumptions.
